category: Geothermal and high-latitude / cold-climate stranded hydro sites attracting energy-intensive industry and datacenters

sites.name: Iceland geothermal fields (Hellisheidi, Nesjavellir, Reykjanes, Krafla, Theistareykir)
sites.region: SW Iceland (Hengill/Reykjanes) and NE Iceland (Krafla/Theistareykir)
sites.capacityGW: 0.76-0.8 GW geothermal (9 plants)
sites.annualTWh: ~6 TWh/yr (geothermal); ~30% of national electricity
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: 40-140 (second-stage field ~40; greenfield first-of-a-kind ~140)
sites.whyStranded: Volcanic island with no grid interconnection to Europe and a tiny domestic population (~390k). Cheap baseload geothermal/hydro had no large local market, so it was historically monetized by importing electro-intensive industry (aluminum) rather than exporting power. The lack of a subsea cable still strands surplus low-cost electricity.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent: cool maritime climate (annual mean ~4-6C) enables near-year-round free-air/seawater cooling; 100% renewable (geothermal+hydro); cheap, stable power; abundant water. Cons: sub-Atlantic latency (~20+ ms to London via subsea fiber FARICE/IRIS/DANICE), seismic and volcanic risk near Reykjanes (active eruptions since 2021), limited surplus headroom (~3.5-4 TWh).
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Geothermal power in Iceland'; National Energy Authority of Iceland (Orkustofnun); IRENA Iceland statistical profile

sites.name: Iceland hydropower (Karahnjukar/Fljotsdalur, Burfell, Hvalfjordur cascade)
sites.region: East Iceland (Karahnjukar) and SW Iceland (Thjorsa/Tungnaa)
sites.capacityGW: ~2.1 GW (≈71% of national capacity)
sites.annualTWh: ~13 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: 30-50 (large legacy hydro; Karahnjukar built explicitly to power Alcoa Fjardaal smelter)
sites.whyStranded: Same island isolation as geothermal. The 690 MW Karahnjukar plant (2007) was built specifically to anchor the Alcoa Fjardaal aluminum smelter at Reydarfjordur because there was no other way to monetize the resource. Aluminum smelters consume ~70-80% of Iceland's electricity.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent climate for cooling (cold, humid maritime air; free cooling year-round) and 100% renewable supply. Operators include Verne Global, atNorth and Borealis Data Center near Keflavik. Cons: latency to mainland markets, limited remaining surplus, dependence on subsea fiber.
sites.source: Askja Energy 'The Energy Sector'; IRENA Iceland profile; reporting on Alcoa Fjardaal / Karahnjukar

sites.name: Olkaria geothermal complex (Olkaria I-VI), Hell's Gate / Greater Olkaria field
sites.region: Rift Valley (Naivasha, Nakuru County)
sites.capacityGW: ~0.95 GW operating (KenGen ~799 MW + Ormat OrPower4 ~150 MW); target 5 GW by 2030
sites.annualTWh: ~6-7 TWh/yr (geothermal supplies ~40-47% of Kenyan electricity)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~50-90 (among the lowest baseload cost on the continent; KenGen expects Olkaria VI to cut national power cost ~18%)
sites.whyStranded: Largest geothermal field in Africa, located in a remote, lightly populated stretch of the Rift Valley. Baseload geothermal far exceeds nearby demand and Kenya periodically curtails or has surplus off-peak power; weak local industrial load and limited regional interconnection historically stranded output. Now targeted to attract data centers and green industry (green hydrogen, e-mobility).
sites.datacenterSuitability: Good: high-altitude equatorial site (~1,900 m) gives mild temperatures and lower air density favorable to evaporative/free cooling; 24/7 renewable baseload at low cost. Microsoft/G42 announced a geothermal-powered AI datacenter near Olkaria (Naivasha). Cons: water competition with agriculture, developing fiber connectivity, single-country political/regulatory risk, seismicity of an active rift.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Olkaria V Geothermal Power Station'; KenGen; trade.gov Kenya geothermal market intelligence; Global Electricity 'Kenya launches Africa's largest geothermal complex'

sites.name: Indonesia geothermal belt (Sarulla, Sorik Marapi, Kamojang, Wayang Windu, Sibayak)
sites.region: Sumatra (North Sumatra, Aceh), West Java, Sulawesi
sites.capacityGW: ~2.7 GW operating (2025); national potential ~23.7 GW over 368 sites; target +5.2 GW
sites.annualTWh: ~16-18 TWh/yr (operating fleet)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~70-130 (PPA-driven; remote Sumatra/Sulawesi fields higher cost)
sites.whyStranded: World's 2nd-largest geothermal potential but most prospects sit on remote, volcanically active islands (Sumatra, Sulawesi, eastern Indonesia) far from Java's demand center and weakly interconnected. The 330 MW Sarulla complex in North Sumatra exemplifies large baseload remote from major load. Government is now urging that data center developers be given access to develop geothermal directly.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Mixed: tropical lowlands are hot/humid (cooling-unfriendly) but highland geothermal sites are cooler; main draw is 24/7 firm renewable baseload to green AI/data-center load near Batam/Sumatra and proximity to the Singapore digital market. Cons: high humidity, seismic/volcanic hazard, grid build-out and fiber needed, permitting complexity.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Geothermal power in Indonesia'; Tempo 'Indonesia's geothermal capacity rises to 2.71 GW'; ANTARA; ThinkGeoEnergy (Sarulla)

sites.name: Norway northern hydropower (Nordland/Troms/Finnmark cascades)
sites.region: Northern Norway and national fleet
sites.capacityGW: ~34 GW national (≈96-99% hydro)
sites.annualTWh: ~154-157 TWh/yr national (record 157.2 TWh in 2024; normal ~137.6 TWh/yr)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~30-50 (legacy reservoir hydro; commercial price historically ~7 EUR-cents/kWh)
sites.whyStranded: Northern Norway has large hydro resources but sparse population and historically limited transmission south/abroad, leaving the north (NO4 price zone) with chronically low, sometimes near-zero, spot prices and surplus power. This cheap green power has attracted aluminum smelters (Hydro/Mosjoen, Sundal) and data centers (e.g. Kolos/Ballangen, Lefdal Mine, Green Mountain).
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent: cold Nordic climate gives year-round free-air cooling, 100% renewable hydro, very low and stable prices in the north, fjord water for cooling, strong fiber. Green Mountain and Lefdal Mine operate large sites. Cons: shrinking surplus (Nordic surplus projected to fall ~90% 2023-2030), grid bottlenecks north-south, rising local opposition to new lines.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Electricity sector in Norway'; SSB; WEF/ArcticToday 'Cryptocurrency miners seek cheap energy in Norway and Sweden'

sites.name: Northern Sweden hydropower (Lule, Skellefte, Ume, Indals rivers) - Lulea/Norrbotten
sites.region: Norrbotten / Vasterbotten (Lulea, Boden, Skelleftea)
sites.capacityGW: ~16.4 GW national hydro
sites.annualTWh: ~65 TWh/yr national (range 55-79 TWh); majority generated in the north
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~30-55 (legacy hydro; commercial price historically ~6.5 EUR-cents/kWh, north zone SE1 often lower)
sites.whyStranded: The big northern rivers generate far more than sparse Norrbotten/Vasterbotten consume; power historically flowed south, and the northern price zones (SE1/SE2) sit well below continental prices. That low-cost surplus drew Facebook's first European datacenter to Lulea (2011/2013) and many bitcoin and colocation operators (Hydro66/Boden, Northern Data). Note: incoming green-steel (H2 Green Steel/Stegra, LKAB/HYBRIT) and battery loads are now absorbing the surplus.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent: among the coldest siting climates in Europe, enabling free-air cooling almost all year; 100% renewable hydro; low northern-zone prices; robust fiber. Meta (Facebook) Lulea, Hydro66/Boden. Cons: surplus eroding fast as electrification ramps; grid capacity for new connections increasingly constrained.
sites.source: Invest in Norrbotten 'Data center'; Statista 'Sweden hydropower capacity 2023'; WEF; RISE 'status of data center and crypto mining energy use in Sweden'

sites.name: British Columbia hydropower (W.A.C. Bennett / G.M. Shrum, Mica, Revelstoke, Site C)
sites.region: British Columbia (Peace River and Columbia River basins)
sites.capacityGW: ~12 GW provincial (BC Hydro); Site C added ~1.1 GW in 2025
sites.annualTWh: ~60-66 TWh/yr provincial (>90% of BC electricity is hydro)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~30-60 (legacy heritage hydro low; Site C new-build much higher, ~80-110)
sites.whyStranded: Large northern reservoir hydro (Peace/Columbia) is remote from southern load and from the small northern population; surplus has historically been exported to the US Pacific Northwest/California at variable prices. Site C's 1.1 GW arrived with limited firm domestic demand, making BC an attractive low-carbon host for new datacenter/industrial load.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent: cool-to-cold interior/northern climate supports free-air cooling; clean firm hydro; strong fiber along the coast and to US; political stability. Existing datacenter clusters in Vancouver/Kamloops. Cons: best surplus is in the remote north away from fiber hubs; transmission to load centers constrained; drought-year reservoir variability.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Hydroelectricity in Canada'; Canadian Mining & Energy 'Top 10 hydroelectric dams in Canada'; reporting on Site C commissioning 2025

sites.name: Manitoba hydropower (Nelson River: Limestone, Long Spruce, Kettle, Keeyask)
sites.region: Manitoba (Nelson River, northern Manitoba)
sites.capacityGW: ~5.7 GW provincial (Manitoba Hydro); Keeyask 695 MW completed 2021-22
sites.annualTWh: ~30-37 TWh/yr (~97% of provincial electricity is hydro)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~25-50 (among the lowest retail/wholesale rates in North America)
sites.whyStranded: Nelson River megaprojects in remote northern Manitoba vastly exceed local demand; power is wheeled ~900 km south via HVDC (Bipole) and exported to the US Midwest (MISO) and Saskatchewan. New Keeyask capacity plus soft export markets leave low-cost surplus that the province is courting for datacenters and green industry.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Excellent: very cold continental winters give long free-cooling season; lowest-cost clean hydro power in North America; stable jurisdiction. Cons: extreme winter and remoteness of the generation in the north; main load/fiber is in Winnipeg far from the dams; export-market dependence.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Hydroelectricity in Canada' / 'List of hydroelectric power stations in Canada'; Manitoba Hydro Keeyask

sites.name: Churchill Falls & proposed Gull Island (Lower Churchill), Labrador
sites.region: Newfoundland and Labrador (Churchill River, Labrador)
sites.capacityGW: 5.43 GW (Churchill Falls); proposed Gull Island ~2.25 GW + expansion under 2024 MOU with Quebec
sites.annualTWh: ~35 TWh/yr (Churchill Falls)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Effective historic price extremely low (~2-3 USD/MWh under the 1969 Hydro-Quebec contract to 2041); new build much higher
sites.whyStranded: Classic stranded-hydro case: one of the largest underground powerhouses in the world sits in near-uninhabited interior Labrador with no local market. Almost all output is locked into a long-term contract selling to Hydro-Quebec at a price now far below market, the textbook example of remote hydro that could not be monetized locally. New Gull Island development and the 2024 Newfoundland-Quebec MOU aim to re-monetize the basin.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Strong on paper: extremely cold subarctic climate (ideal free cooling), huge firm clean hydro block, and abundant water. Cons: extreme remoteness and harsh winters, almost no existing fiber or population, output contractually committed to Quebec until 2041, limited evacuation transmission, transmission-gap is the core constraint.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Hydroelectricity in Canada'; reporting on Churchill Falls Generating Station and 2024 NL-Hydro-Quebec MOU / Gull Island

sites.name: Itaipu Dam (binational) + Yacyreta + Acaray surplus
sites.region: Parana River (Itaipu, border with Brazil) and Parana (Yacyreta, border with Argentina)
sites.capacityGW: Itaipu 14 GW (Paraguay entitled to half ~7 GW) + Yacyreta 3.2 GW + Acaray 0.23 GW
sites.annualTWh: ~32 TWh/yr Paraguayan surplus; Itaipu produced ~37.3 TWh in H1 2025; Paraguay exports >50% of its generation
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~10-50 (surplus historically sold to Brazil at subsidized ~10 USD/MWh; industrial tariff ~37-50 USD/MWh)
sites.whyStranded: Paraguay (pop. ~7M) consumes only a fraction of its half of Itaipu; for decades the surplus was ceded/sold cheaply to Brazil under the binational treaty at near-cost prices rather than used domestically, the archetypal stranded hydro surplus. That ~32 TWh/yr of underpriced power has pulled in bitcoin miners (HIVE, Penguin/Sazmining); Paraguay reached ~4% of global hashrate (#4) by 2026.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Mixed: huge cheap firm hydro and surplus, but subtropical hot/humid climate (poor for free cooling, raises PUE) and historically thin international fiber. Strong for crypto/HPC where cooling is engineered; weaker for latency-sensitive cloud. Cons: heat/humidity, fiber and grid-buildout needs, evolving regulation of mining tariffs.
sites.source: Hashrate Index 'State of Bitcoin Mining in Paraguay 2026'; Decrypt (Sazmining/Itaipu); Bit2me on surplus mining; MoveToParaguay mining guide

sites.name: Bhutan hydropower (Tala, Chukha, Mangdechhu, Punatsangchhu) + Gedu/Jigmeling mining
sites.region: Western/Central Bhutan (Wangchhu, Mangdechhu, Punatsangchhu basins); mining at Gedu and Jigmeling
sites.capacityGW: ~3.5 GW operating; national potential ~33 GW (domestic peak demand only ~1 GW)
sites.annualTWh: ~10-11 TWh/yr; large monsoon-season surplus
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~25-50 (low-cost run-of-river/storage hydro; export price to India set by PPAs)
sites.whyStranded: Landlocked Himalayan country whose run-of-river hydro produces big monsoon-season surpluses far above the ~1 GW domestic demand; surplus is exported to India, but at low PPA rates and curtailed/spilled when Indian demand is soft. To capture more value, the state used summer surplus for government Bitcoin mining (Bitdeer partnership: 100 MW Gedu, +500 MW Jigmeling by 2026), accumulating ~13,000 BTC.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Strong on climate: high-altitude Himalayan sites are cold (excellent free cooling) with 100% renewable hydro. Cons: monsoonal seasonality (winter dry-season power shortfall, even imports), mountainous remoteness, limited international fiber and grid evacuation, and a 2025 strategic pivot, Bhutan sold ~70% of its BTC and appears to have wound down state mining in favor of direct exports to India.
sites.source: Cointelegraph 'How Bhutan is building a green Bitcoin economy'; Al Jazeera 'Why is Bhutan betting on crypto'; ORF analysis; Dailyhunt/CryptoRank on 2025 BTC selldown

sites.name: Nepal Himalayan hydropower (Upper Tamakoshi, Tanahu, run-of-river fleet)
sites.region: Central/Eastern Himalaya (Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali basins)
sites.capacityGW: ~2.6-3.2 GW operating (Dec 2023 ~2.64 GW); techno-economic potential ~42 GW (theoretical ~83 GW)
sites.annualTWh: Exports ~2.35 TWh to India in FY2024/25; ~3.8 TWh projected wet-season surplus by 2028
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~40-70 (run-of-river build cost; export realized ~ Indian market/PPA prices)
sites.whyStranded: Predominantly run-of-river hydro produces large wet-season (monsoon) surpluses that exceed domestic demand and Indian export approvals, forcing curtailment/spill: IPPAN estimated ~USD 192M of curtailed energy in FY2024/25. Cross-border export to India is capped by approvals and transmission, stranding monsoon power. Promoters eye green hydrogen and data/crypto load to absorb the wet-season surplus.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Strong on climate: mid/high-altitude sites are cool (good free cooling) and power is 100% renewable. Cons: severe seasonality (winter dry-season deficit and imports), seismic hazard (2015 earthquake zone), mountainous terrain, immature international fiber and grid, and reliance on Indian transmission and policy, making it best suited to flexible/interruptible loads.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Energy in Nepal'; NREL 'Cross-Border Energy Trade between Nepal and India'; ScienceDirect 'Green hydrogen from surplus hydroelectric power: Nepal'; Rising Nepal Daily on exports/curtailment

caveats: Coordinates are representative centroids of the resource region or flagship project, not a single point of generation; large hydro/geothermal basins span tens of kilometers. Capacity and generation figures are the latest I could source (2023-2026) but mix national totals (e.g., Norway 34 GW / 154-157 TWh; Sweden 16.4 GW / ~65 TWh; Canada provincial fleets) with specific projects (Sarulla 330 MW, Churchill Falls 5.43 GW, Itaipu 14 GW). Where a number is a national fleet rather than the named stranded sub-region, the text says so. LCOE values are indicative ranges, not audited figures: legacy reservoir/geothermal hydro is genuinely cheap (often 25-50 USD/MWh), but realized/contract prices (e.g., Churchill Falls' ~2-3 USD/MWh to Hydro-Quebec, Itaipu's ~10 USD/MWh subsidized export, northern Nordic near-zero spot) reflect contractual/market conditions rather than true LCOE; new-build (Site C, greenfield geothermal) is substantially higher. 'Stranded' is used loosely to mean curtailed, exported at depressed prices, or remote from load/fiber, not legally stranded assets. Key dynamics that erode the 'stranded surplus' thesis: the Nordic surplus is projected to fall ~90% from 2023 to 2030 as electrification (green steel, batteries, EVs) and datacenters absorb it; Iceland's remaining surplus is only ~3.5-4 TWh; Bhutan pivoted in 2025 away from state Bitcoin mining (sold ~70% of holdings) toward direct exports to India. Datacenter suitability is qualitative; cold/cool high-latitude and high-altitude sites are genuinely excellent for free-air/water cooling, but tropical surplus sites (Paraguay, lowland Indonesia) are hot/humid and suit engineered-cooling crypto/HPC more than latency-sensitive cloud. Several figures come from secondary aggregators (Wikipedia, trade press, Statista) rather than primary utility filings; treat medium-confidence entries (Canadian provincial breakdowns, Nepal/Bhutan seasonal surplus, LCOE bands) as order-of-magnitude. Bitcoin-mining hashrate and crypto-treasury figures are fast-moving and may have shifted since the cited 2025-2026 reports.

category: Regions with large curtailed/overbuilt variable renewables (wind/solar) where electricity is frequently spilled or priced near/below zero — candidate hosts for flexible AI compute loads

sites.name: Xinjiang renewable base (Hami/Junggar/Turpan, incl. Midong 3.5 GW solar)
sites.region: Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (Northwest grid)
sites.capacityGW: ~104.8 GW total new-energy installed end-2024 (wind ~38 GW, solar ~43+ GW mid-2024, rising fast); +35.6 GW added in 2024 alone
sites.annualTWh: ~10-18 TWh/yr strandable; solar curtailment reported 12-18% (locally up to ~21%), wind several %; solar curtailment ~5.7% nationally H1-2025 with Xinjiang among worst by volume and rate
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Utility solar/wind LCOE ~$15-30/MWh; intra-day surplus and provincial spot floor prices fall toward zero during midday solar peaks
sites.whyStranded: Resource sits >2,000 km from load centers in east/central China; UHV DC export lines (e.g., Hami-Zhengzhou) and local grid cannot evacuate all output, so surplus is curtailed (offloaded) especially midday and in spring/autumn low-demand periods
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheap surplus power, vast cheap land, cool nights/winters, dry air aiding evaporative-free cooling, designated 'East Data West Compute' (东数西算) national node. Cons: extreme summer heat (Turpan >40C), very low water/arid (cooling water scarce), seismic in places, political/sanctions risk on Xinjiang-linked supply chains, long-haul fiber latency to coast
sites.source: Ember China Energy Transition Review 2025; China Daily; Global Energy Monitor; Power-Technology / Bloomberg curtailment coverage

sites.name: Inner Mongolia large-scale wind & solar bases (Kubuqi/Ordos, Bayannur)
sites.region: Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (West & North grids)
sites.capacityGW: ~135 GW cumulative new-energy installed (now exceeds thermal); six approved mega-bases totaling ~72 GW planned
sites.annualTWh: ~10-15 TWh/yr strandable; among the largest curtailment provinces by absolute volume; national wind curtailment ~6.6% H1-2025 (Inner Mongolia above average)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Wind/solar LCOE ~$15-30/MWh; surplus and midday/overnight troughs push local marginal value toward zero
sites.whyStranded: Generation far outpaces local demand and inter-provincial transmission; West Inner Mongolia grid is partially islanded; UHV lines to Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and Shandong are saturated at peaks, forcing curtailment of the world's largest land-based wind farms
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: very cheap power and land, cold dry climate (long free-cooling season), flat terrain, proximity to Beijing fiber, established hyperscale clusters (Ulanqab, Hohhot - Alibaba/Huawei). Cons: water scarcity, dust storms, summer dust/heat spikes, coal-grid carbon accounting concerns
sites.source: CREA case study (clean energy bases Inner Mongolia 2024); Global Times; Ember 2025; 36Kr

sites.name: Gansu Hexi Corridor wind/solar base (Jiuquan/Dunhuang)
sites.region: Gansu Province (Northwest grid)
sites.capacityGW: ~64 GW total new-energy installed end-2024 (+12 GW in 2024); 36% of provincial electricity from wind+solar in 2024
sites.annualTWh: ~5-10 TWh/yr strandable; Gansu among the highest curtailment-rate provinces in H1-2025 (historically the original 'curtailment capital', once ~30%+ wind curtailment in 2016-17)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: LCOE ~$15-30/MWh; local spot prices fall near zero in spring midday solar surplus
sites.whyStranded: Jiuquan wind base was built faster than the Hexi-to-central transmission corridor; even with UHV DC (Jiuquan-Hunan) the export capacity lags installed GW, causing periodic spilling
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheap surplus power, cheap arid land, cool/dry, part of national west-compute corridor. Cons: severe water scarcity, remoteness, dust, long fiber distance to coastal demand
sites.source: Ember China Energy Transition Review 2025; Renewable Energy World; Lantau Group; Oxford Energy Chinese climate policy

sites.name: Qinghai Talatan / Gonghe / Golmud solar-wind-CSP hybrid base
sites.region: Qinghai Province (Northwest grid)
sites.capacityGW: Tens of GW (Talatan one of the world's largest PV parks); ~46% of provincial electricity from wind+solar in 2024; ~1.6 GW molten-salt CSP centered on Golmud/Gonghe/Dachaidan
sites.annualTWh: ~3-8 TWh/yr strandable; Qinghai solar curtailment rose to 15.2% in H1-2025 (from 8.8% prior year)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Solar LCOE ~$15-25/MWh (high plateau irradiance); local prices toward zero in daytime surplus
sites.whyStranded: High-altitude plateau, very low local demand, single UHV export (Qinghai-Henan); rapid PV buildout outran evacuation capacity, driving rising daytime curtailment
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: very cool ambient (high altitude aids free cooling), low population, cheap solar, CSP+storage can firm supply, designated west-compute node. Cons: altitude ~3,000 m reduces air-cooling density and stresses hardware, thin air and low humidity, remoteness, water limits, seismic plateau
sites.source: Ember 2025; ASME CSP in China 2025 review; Power-Technology / pv-tech curtailment coverage

sites.name: West Texas / ERCOT West zone & Panhandle (Permian-edge solar+wind)
sites.region: West Texas / ERCOT West and Panhandle zones
sites.capacityGW: ERCOT-wide wind+solar ~65 GW (2025), heading to ~109 GW by 2030; West/Panhandle hosts a large share
sites.annualTWh: ~8 TWh/yr curtailed ERCOT-wide in 2024 (West zone ~3.1 TWh wind + ~2.2 TWh solar); West Texas solar = ~22% of all ERCOT renewable curtailment; worst sites lose ~20-60% of output (e.g., a Los Vientos unit: 4,430 curtailment hours in 2024)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Wind/solar LCOE ~$20-35/MWh; West Texas/Panhandle real-time hub prices frequently dip negative midday (solar) and in high-wind hours
sites.whyStranded: West Texas Export constraint: surplus cannot move east to DFW/Houston load; local transmission saturated, especially Jan-Apr low-demand/maintenance season, producing congestion and negative local prices
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: deregulated ERCOT market easy to interconnect flexible load, cheap land, abundant cheap surplus power, existing Permian gas+fiber, crypto/AI miners already co-located, no state income tax. Cons: extreme summer heat (drives cooling load and grid scarcity pricing/curtailment-of-load risk), water scarcity in arid west, occasional grid-reliability events (winter storms)
sites.source: Modo Energy ERCOT curtailment research; U.S. EIA Today in Energy

sites.name: Atacama / Antofagasta northern Chile solar cluster (SEN north)
sites.region: Antofagasta / Atacama regions, northern Chile
sites.capacityGW: Multi-GW solar concentrated in the north; national solar+wind growing rapidly (Atacama Oasis and other mega-projects in pipeline; >20 GW developer queue)
sites.annualTWh: ~5.9 TWh curtailed in 2024 (mostly northern solar+wind) = ~19% of solar+wind output; up 121% from ~2.7 TWh in 2023; cumulative curtailment losses ~$562M since 2022
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: World-record-low solar LCOE: sub-$20-30/MWh in Atacama (e.g., historical $29.1/MWh auction bid); northern nodal spot prices frequently collapse to ~$0 midday
sites.whyStranded: Best irradiance on Earth but load (Santiago/industry) is >1,000 km south; the north-south transmission backbone (Kimal-Lo Aguirre HVDC under build) is insufficient, so northern solar is spilled when the link saturates
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: unmatched solar resource, very cheap daytime power, stable cool coastal climate near Antofagasta, mining-industry power infrastructure, subsea cable landings for connectivity. Cons: extreme desert water scarcity (cooling), high altitude inland sites, seismic (Pacific Ring of Fire), distance to major fiber hubs
sites.source: Ember (reducing curtailment in Chile); pv magazine; PV Tech; Wikipedia 'Curtailment in Chile'

sites.name: South Australia wind & solar fleet (mid-north / Eyre Peninsula)
sites.region: South Australia (NEM)
sites.capacityGW: ~6+ GW large-scale wind+solar plus heavy rooftop PV; renewables met 100% of SA demand for 27% of 2024 (~99 days)
sites.annualTWh: ~4.5 TWh large-scale wind+solar curtailed in 2024; large-solar economic offloading reached ~59% of potential output in Q4-2024
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Wind/solar LCOE ~A$40-60/MWh; SA wholesale prices hit zero/negative in roughly half of dispatch intervals in late-2025 midday windows
sites.whyStranded: SA is at the end of the NEM with limited interconnection to Victoria (Heywood); when local wind+solar+rooftop exceed demand and the interconnector saturates, large generators are curtailed and prices go negative (the new Project EnergyConnect to NSW aims to ease this)
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: world-leading instantaneous renewable share, frequent zero/negative midday prices ideal for interruptible compute, temperate climate, political stability, strong policy support. Cons: smaller grid (load-balancing limits), water constraints in arid state, distance from Asia-Pacific fiber hubs adds latency, summer heatwaves
sites.source: RenewEconomy; AEMO South Australian Electricity Report Dec 2024; pv-tech

sites.name: Scotland onshore + offshore wind (Seagreen, Moray, central belt north of B6)
sites.region: Scotland (north of the B6 transmission boundary)
sites.capacityGW: Scotland hosts the bulk of GB onshore wind plus major offshore (Seagreen ~1.1 GW, Moray East/West, etc.); GB offshore wind ~15+ GW with large Scottish share
sites.annualTWh: ~8.3 TWh of wind curtailed across GB in 2024 (98% paid to Scottish wind); constraint payments >£393M in 2024 (rose from £310M/4.3 TWh in 2023); Seagreen alone ~40% of constraint volume
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Offshore wind CfD strike prices roughly £45-75/MWh (~$55-95/MWh); during constraints generators are paid to switch off (negative effective value) while gas redispatches south
sites.whyStranded: The B6 (Scotland-England) boundary and B4 are chronically congested (34% and 42% constrained in 2025); Scottish wind output exceeds export capability to English demand, so it is curtailed pending new HVDC links (Eastern Green Link 1/2)
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool maritime climate (excellent free cooling, minimal water), abundant cheap surplus wind, low ambient temps year-round, strong subsea fiber landings, stable jurisdiction. Cons: high electricity retail/levies, grid connection queue delays, planning constraints, higher labor/construction costs, transmission charging (TNUoS) penalizes northern siting
sites.source: Modo Energy GB constraints research; Energy Voice; UKERC; RenewableUK

sites.name: California Central Valley / Mojave solar (CAISO)
sites.region: California (CAISO) - Central Valley and southern desert
sites.capacityGW: ~28.2 GW utility-scale wind+solar PV end-2024 (from 9.7 GW in 2014), plus very large behind-the-meter rooftop PV
sites.annualTWh: ~3.4 TWh (3.4 million MWh) utility-scale wind+solar curtailed in 2024 (+29% YoY); solar = ~93% of curtailed energy
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Utility solar LCOE ~$25-40/MWh; ~1,180 hours (~13% of 2024 hours) had below-zero wholesale prices (up from ~530 hours/6% in 2023) driven by the deepening 'duck curve'
sites.whyStranded: Midday solar oversupply collapses net demand (down ~45% since 2020 in 9am-3pm window); local transmission and limited export plus must-take solar force curtailment and negative prices around midday
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: deep midday surplus perfect for daytime-flexible compute, mature data-center market and fiber, strong PPA/clean-energy ecosystem. Cons: high land/power retail costs, strict water/environmental permitting, wildfire and PSPS grid risk, evening net-peak scarcity (the cheap power is only midday), high cost of doing business
sites.source: U.S. EIA Today in Energy; gridstatus.io; REsurety

sites.name: Spain / Iberia solar+wind (Extremadura, Castilla, Andalucia)
sites.region: Iberian peninsula (central/southern Spain)
sites.capacityGW: Solar PV ~40 GW by end-2025 (now Spain's largest technology; +7.2 GW in 2024, record ~8.4 GW in 2025), plus ~30 GW wind
sites.annualTWh: Curtailment ~2% in 2024, projected to rise toward ~5% by 2027-2028; >800 hours of zero/negative prices in 2024 (matched within first 9 months of 2025)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Solar LCOE ~$20-35/MWh; average price during zero/negative hours fell from about -EUR0.12/MWh (2024) toward -EUR1.80/MWh (2025); 400+ negative-price hours in spring 2025
sites.whyStranded: Iberia is a weakly interconnected 'electrical island' (limited cross-Pyrenees links to France ~<5% of capacity); midday solar surplus cannot be exported, collapsing daytime prices and forcing curtailment (the April 2025 blackout underscored low-inertia stress)
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheap abundant midday solar, growing data-center hubs (Madrid, Aragon - AWS/Microsoft/Meta investing), good Atlantic/Med subsea fiber, EU jurisdiction. Cons: hot dry summers and water-stress (cooling and drought permitting), grid-stability/inertia concerns after 2025 blackout, interconnection queue limits, evening price recovery
sites.source: Modo Energy Iberia/Spain research; WeMake Consultores; pv magazine; Strategic Energy Europe

sites.name: Northern Scandinavia (northern Sweden SE1/SE2, northern Norway NO4)
sites.region: Northern Sweden (SE1/SE2) and northern Norway (NO4), Nordic grid
sites.capacityGW: Large hydro reservoirs plus substantial onshore wind (SE1/SE2 are structural surplus zones); exact wind GW growing with northern buildout (e.g., Markbygden cluster ~hundreds of MW to >1 GW)
sites.annualTWh: Persistent surplus rather than headline curtailment TWh; northern zones (SE1/SE2/NO4) routinely see lowest Nordic prices and frequent near-zero/negative hours during wet/windy low-demand periods
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Onshore wind LCOE ~EUR25-40/MWh; northern Nordic spot prices regularly fall to ~EUR0-10/MWh and go negative when hydro inflows + wind exceed limited south-bound transfer
sites.whyStranded: Generation-rich north lacks sufficient HVAC/HVDC transfer capacity to southern (SE3/SE4) and continental demand; bottlenecks split the market into low-price northern and higher-price southern zones, stranding northern surplus
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cold climate (best-in-class free cooling, minimal cooling energy), 100% low-carbon power, very cheap surplus, abundant water/hydro, strong fiber, stable jurisdictions; already a hyperscale magnet (Lulea/Boden Sweden - Meta, H2 Green Steel; northern Norway). Cons: long fiber latency to continental Europe, dark/cold winters for staffing logistics, grid-connection lead times, sparse local labor
sites.source: Montel; Energy Exemplar Nordic market; RatedPower grid congestion in the Nordics; Statista Nordic prices

caveats: Numbers are best-available point estimates assembled from secondary sources (May 2026) and should be treated as approximate; verify against primary regulator/operator data before investment use. Key caveats: (1) China provincial figures mix "new-energy installed capacity" (which sometimes includes storage) with wind+solar specifically, and Chinese curtailment statistics are widely believed to understate true spilling (official methodology counts only above a ~5% threshold and excludes some pre-curtailment); H1-2025 rates (solar ~5.7%, wind ~6.6% national; Xinjiang/Qinghai/Gansu 12-18%+) are rising as buildout outpaces grid. (2) Curtailment is volatile year-to-year and is actively being reduced by new UHV/HVDC lines (China), Project EnergyConnect (South Australia), Eastern Green Links (Scotland), Kimal-Lo Aguirre HVDC (Chile), and batteries (Texas, Chile, Spain) — so "strandable" energy at any site may shrink within a few years. (3) Coordinates are representative centroids of a resource region or flagship project, not a specific parcel. (4) LCOE and "near-zero/negative price" figures are indicative ranges; negative-price hour counts are nodal/zonal and differ from system averages. (5) "Datacenter suitability" weighs water, cooling-climate, altitude, seismicity, connectivity and political risk qualitatively — the cheapest curtailed power often coincides with the worst water/remoteness/latency tradeoffs (especially Xinjiang, Gansu, Qinghai, Atacama). (6) The Nordics show structural low/negative northern-zone prices more than large reported curtailment TWh; reported TWh for that region was not pinned to a single authoritative figure. Highest-confidence quantitative entries: ERCOT/West Texas, CAISO, South Australia, Scotland, Chile, Spain (operator/EIA/AEMO/Modo/Ember-grade sources). Medium-confidence: the four Chinese provinces and the Nordics.

category: Desert / frontier solar & wind megaproject zones with vast low-cost generation potential but weak local demand and limited transmission — candidate regions for siting AI/compute load near stranded or curtailment-prone renewable power.

sites.name: Noor Ouarzazate Solar Complex (Drâa-Tafilalet)
sites.region: Drâa-Tafilalet (Ouarzazate / pre-Saharan plateau)
sites.capacityGW: 0.58 GW operating (CSP+PV); regional pre-Saharan PV/CSP potential tens of GW
sites.annualTWh: ~1.1 TWh/yr (existing complex); regional desert potential >100 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: CSP ~$0.12-0.19/kWh (early 2010s tariffs, high for CSP); modern Moroccan PV bids ~$25-40/MWh
sites.whyStranded: Sited on high pre-Saharan plateau far from coastal demand centers (Casablanca/Rabat) and from Europe; Morocco's domestic peak demand (~7 GW) is small relative to exploitable desert resource. CSP was expensive; cheap PV expansion outpaces local load.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: superb DNI/GHI, abundant flat land, EU-proximate fiber via Morocco landing stations, relatively stable governance. Cons: hot semi-arid summers (40C+) raise cooling load; acute water scarcity (dam-fed, drought-stressed) limits evaporative cooling — dry/liquid cooling required; moderate seismicity in Atlas region.
sites.source: Power Technology project profile; Wikipedia Ouarzazate Solar Power Station; World Bank Noor case study

sites.name: Xlinks Morocco-UK Power Project (Guelmim-Oued Noun)
sites.region: Guelmim-Oued Noun (southern Atlantic Sahara coast)
sites.capacityGW: 11.5 GW (7.5 GW solar + 4 GW wind) + 5 GW/22.5 GWh battery
sites.annualTWh: ~26-30 TWh/yr planned export to GB
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Announced delivered CfD of GBP 48/MWh (~$60/MWh) to UK incl. 3,800 km HVDC subsea; underlying generation LCOE far lower (~$30-40/MWh)
sites.whyStranded: Entire output designed for export to Britain via 3,800 km HVDC cable, not local use — local southern-Morocco demand is negligible. UK government declined to fund/CfD the interconnector (2025), leaving 11.5 GW of resource without a contracted offtaker — classic stranded export asset.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: co-located solar+wind (strong diurnal complementarity) plus 22.5 GWh storage gives near-firm power; Atlantic coast moderates heat and enables seawater cooling; existing planned grid/fiber buildout. Cons: very remote desert, limited existing fiber backbone, water-scarce interior, political/financing uncertainty after UK pullout.
sites.source: Xlinks; Wikipedia Xlinks Morocco-UK Power Project; PV-Tech (UK declines CfD, 2025)

sites.name: NEOM Green Hydrogen / Oxagon (Tabuk, NW Saudi Arabia)
sites.region: Tabuk Province (NEOM, Red Sea coast)
sites.capacityGW: ~4 GW dedicated (2.2 GW solar + 1.6 GW wind) for green-H2; NEOM zone targets far more
sites.annualTWh: ~8-10 TWh/yr (4 GW at high MENA capacity factors)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Saudi solar record bids $10.40-13.50/MWh (Al Shuaibah 2 / Fasiliyah); NEOM blended solar+wind for H2 est. ~$20-30/MWh
sites.whyStranded: NEOM sits in an empty NW desert with almost no pre-existing load; the 4 GW was built specifically to make export ammonia, and Saudi Arabia's grid is still ~98% fossil with localized solar curtailment (>12% midday in Northern Borders, 2025). Vast resource, thin local grid/demand.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: among world's cheapest solar; Oxagon AI datacenter (DataVolt, 1.5 GW, $5bn) already planned using Red Sea seawater cooling for net-zero/no-freshwater operation; new fiber/port infrastructure. Cons: extreme heat (45C+) raises cooling energy; fresh water essentially absent (desalination needed); concentrated political/single-jurisdiction risk.
sites.source: ACWA Power / NGHC; NEOM-DataVolt Oxagon announcement; Energy & Utilities (Saudi record solar tariffs)

sites.name: Sudair Solar PV (Riyadh Province)
sites.region: Sudair Industrial City, Riyadh Province (Najd plateau)
sites.capacityGW: 1.5 GW operating (one of Saudi's largest single PV plants)
sites.annualTWh: ~3.5 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: PPA ~$12.4/MWh (1.24 c/kWh class); national record bids down to $10.40/MWh
sites.whyStranded: Interior Najd desert location; Saudi solar already triggers midday curtailment as PV outpaces flexible demand and grid evacuation. Generation is cheap but local daytime demand is dominated by AC peaks that don't fully absorb spring/autumn solar surplus.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: ultra-cheap firmable solar, flat land, proximity to Riyadh fiber/cloud regions (AWS, Oracle, Google KSA zones). Cons: extreme continental desert heat (45-50C summer), no surface water — desalinated/recycled water or dry cooling mandatory; daytime-only solar requires storage/grid firming for 24x7 compute.
sites.source: ACWA Power Sudair; Balkan Green Energy News; Reneweconomy (Saudi record low 1.04c/kWh)

sites.name: Al Dhafra Solar PV (Abu Dhabi)
sites.region: Al Dhafra region, Abu Dhabi Emirate
sites.capacityGW: 2.0 GW operating (world's largest single-site PV at 2023 opening)
sites.annualTWh: ~4.3 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Record-low PPA ~$13.2-13.5/MWh (AED 4.85 fils/kWh) at financial close
sites.whyStranded: Less 'stranded' than remote sites (Abu Dhabi grid is strong), but it exemplifies a desert zone where record-cheap daytime solar far exceeds what flexible daytime load absorbs without storage; surplus midday PV is a prime candidate for compute load-shifting. Resource (GHI) regionally vast vs. UAE's modest population/demand.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: world-record cheap solar; UAE is already a Gulf datacenter/AI hub (G42, Microsoft, fiber-rich, subsea cable landings); strong grid and capital. Cons: very high heat/humidity near coast (45C, high dewpoint) penalizes cooling efficiency; freshwater scarce (desalination-dependent); land for very large campuses limited near the coast.
sites.source: EWEC/Masdar Al Dhafra factsheet; AGBI; Renewables Now (record-low tariff)

sites.name: Benban Solar Park (Aswan)
sites.region: Aswan Governorate, Western Desert (~40 km NW of Aswan)
sites.capacityGW: ~1.65-1.8 GW operating across 41 plots
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Feed-in-tariff PPAs $71-84/MWh (2017-era FIT, high vs. modern bids); newer Egyptian PV nearer $20-30/MWh
sites.whyStranded: Remote Upper-Egypt desert ~650 km south of Cairo, far from main load; relies on 220/500 kV lines to Aswan. Egyptian grid congestion and a load center concentrated in the north leave Upper-Egypt solar partly transmission-constrained. Strong export ambition (to Europe via Egypt-Greece/Saudi interconnectors) underscores weak local absorption.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: excellent DNI, vast cheap desert land, adjacent High Aswan Dam hydro (firming + cooling water from Nile/Lake Nasser), improving subsea fiber (Egypt is a global cable chokepoint). Cons: extreme summer heat in Upper Egypt (40-45C); Nile water is politically/agriculturally contested; political and currency risk.
sites.source: Wikipedia Benban Solar Park; EIB SESA; pv magazine (Egyptian PV expansion)

sites.name: Hyphen / Tsau Khaeb Green Hydrogen Zone (Lüderitz)
sites.region: Tsau //Khaeb National Park, ǁKaras Region (Sperrgebiet, near Lüderitz)
sites.capacityGW: 5-7 GW renewables (e.g. ~3.5 GW solar + ~4 GW wind feeding 3 GW electrolysis); ~4,000 km2 site
sites.annualTWh: ~25-35 TWh/yr at full build (very high combined CF: solar ~32%, wind ~60%)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Among world's best combined solar+wind resource; blended LCOE est. ~$25-40/MWh (project-stage)
sites.whyStranded: One of the planet's strongest co-located solar+wind resources sits in a near-uninhabited desert/restricted diamond zone. Namibia's entire national demand is only ~0.6 GW, so domestic load can absorb almost none of a multi-GW build; entire rationale is export (green ammonia/H2). Essentially zero local transmission or demand.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool dry Atlantic-coast climate (Benguela current) gives low ambient temps and excellent free/air + seawater cooling — rare among desert sites; exceptional firm renewable profile (day solar + strong reliable wind) ideal for 24x7 compute; planned port/desal/power buildout. Cons: extremely remote, minimal existing fiber (would need new subsea/terrestrial cable), sensitive national-park siting, nascent grid.
sites.source: Hyphen Hydrogen Energy; Green Hydrogen Organisation (Namibia); Ammonia Energy Association

sites.name: Boegoebaai Green Hydrogen Hub / Northern Cape REDZ8
sites.region: Northern Cape (Boegoebaai, ~60 km N of Port Nolloth; REDZ8 / Springbok zone)
sites.capacityGW: ~9-10 GW solar+wind planned (supporting ~5 GW electrolysis); Northern Cape REDZ host vast further GW
sites.annualTWh: ~25-30 TWh/yr planned; Northern Cape resource potential many tens of TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: South African REIPPPP solar/wind bids historically ~$20-50/MWh; Northern Cape among cheapest
sites.whyStranded: Northern Cape has South Africa's best irradiation and good wind but is sparsely populated and remote from Gauteng load; grid evacuation is severely transmission-constrained (Eskom queue saturation in the Cape REDZ is a recognized bottleneck), forcing curtailment/connection delays. Boegoebaai's output is aimed at export H2, not local demand.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: excellent combined solar+wind, cool semi-arid Atlantic-influenced climate moderating heat, planned port/desal at Boegoebaai for seawater cooling, English-speaking jurisdiction with established IPP framework. Cons: very water-scarce interior; chronic national grid instability/loadshedding history; transmission build lag; remoteness/fiber gaps.
sites.source: Mining Weekly (Northern Cape H2 hub); GH2 South Africa; CSIR environmental assessment

sites.name: Australia-Asia PowerLink / Powell Creek Renewable Energy Zone (Sun Cable)
sites.region: Barkly Region, Northern Territory (Powell Creek / outback)
sites.capacityGW: 17-20 GW solar + 36-42 GWh storage (world's largest planned PV + battery)
sites.annualTWh: ~40+ TWh/yr potential; ~10 TWh/yr targeted for export (1.75 GW to Singapore)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Australian outback utility PV LCOE ~$25-40/MWh; delivered Singapore export far higher due to 4,300 km HVDC subsea
sites.whyStranded: Built in near-empty NT outback explicitly because there is essentially no local demand; needs an 800 km line just to reach Darwin and a 4,300 km subsea cable to reach Singapore's market. The vast majority of 17-20 GW has no local offtake — the entire economic premise is long-distance export.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: world-class solar, enormous flat cheap land, massive co-located battery (firming for 24x7 compute), stable jurisdiction, planned Darwin (Middle Arm) industrial precinct with fiber. Cons: tropical-savanna heat and wet-season humidity near Darwin; extreme remoteness of Powell Creek; very limited inland water and fiber; cyclone exposure near the coast.
sites.source: Wikipedia Australia-Asia Power Link; RenewEconomy (Sun Cable expansion / Indonesia approval); SMEC

sites.name: Australian Renewable Energy Hub (AREH), Pilbara
sites.region: Pilbara, Western Australia (~6,500 km2 near Port Hedland)
sites.capacityGW: 26 GW (combined wind + solar)
sites.annualTWh: ~80-90 TWh/yr potential at full build
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Pilbara solar+wind LCOE est. ~$25-40/MWh; blended firm renewable competitive
sites.whyStranded: 26 GW in a remote mining desert with tiny local population; designed to make ~1.6 Mt/yr green hydrogen/ammonia and green iron for export, not local consumption. Needs a new Pilbara Green Link transmission corridor (Great Sandy Desert) just to reach Port Hedland — no existing large grid to absorb it.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: huge co-located solar+wind (good firming), proximity to Port Hedland (port, fiber landing, industrial offtake), Major Project / Priority status, very stable jurisdiction. Cons: extreme Pilbara heat (often 45C+) heavily penalizes cooling; cyclone-prone coast; arid interior water scarcity; fiber/transmission still to be built.
sites.source: Wikipedia Australian Renewable Energy Hub; pv magazine Australia (26 GW federal backing 2026); CSIRO HyResource

sites.name: Gobi Desert Renewable Mega-Bases (China)
sites.region: Inner Mongolia / Gansu / Ningxia / Xinjiang / Qinghai (Gobi & desertified lands)
sites.capacityGW: ~455 GW of solar+wind base capacity planned/under construction by 2030 (~60% solar, 40% wind)
sites.annualTWh: ~800-900+ TWh/yr at full build (order-of-magnitude)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: China utility-scale solar LCOE world-lowest ~$27-33/MWh (2024-2025); Gobi base solar among cheapest globally
sites.whyStranded: Generation is concentrated in sparsely populated northwestern deserts while demand sits in the eastern/coastal provinces; despite UHV transmission buildout, northwest provinces have historically suffered solar/wind curtailment (Xinjiang/Gansu double-digit curtailment in peak periods) because local load and evacuation capacity lag installed capacity.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheapest solar on Earth, vast flat land, cold/dry winters reduce cooling load, China's 'East Data West Compute' (Dong Shu Xi Suan) policy explicitly steers datacenters to these western renewable hubs; existing UHV + fiber backbones. Cons: water scarcity in Gobi limits evaporative cooling; large summer-winter and diurnal temperature swings; sandstorm/dust exposure; export/geopolitical and data-sovereignty constraints for non-Chinese users.
sites.source: SCMP (Gobi/western build equals half US capacity); gov.cn (455 GW mega-bases); Wood Mackenzie / PV-Tech (China LCOE)

sites.name: Mongolian Gobi / Gobitec Zone
sites.region: Gobi Desert (southern Mongolia)
sites.capacityGW: ~100 GW proposed under Gobitec; technical resource far larger
sites.annualTWh: ~2,600 TWh/yr theoretical solar+wind potential in the Gobi
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Project-stage; strong resource implies low LCOE (~$25-45/MWh) but limited buildout to date
sites.whyStranded: Mongolia's entire grid demand is ~1.5 GW, a rounding error against a 2,600 TWh/yr resource. There is essentially no domestic offtake and only weak interconnection; Gobitec's whole premise is exporting via a not-yet-built Asian Supergrid to China/Korea/Japan. Almost entirely stranded today.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: enormous low-cost solar+wind, cold climate (very low cooling energy, strong free-cooling for much of year), vast empty land. Cons: extreme winter cold and large temperature swings, very thin transmission and fiber, landlocked with limited connectivity, harsh logistics, dust/sandstorms, governance/financing risk. Best suited if power is consumed in-situ by compute rather than exported.
sites.source: Energy Charter / UNESCAP Gobitec & Asian Supergrid reports

sites.name: Hyrasia One / Mangystau Green Energy Zone
sites.region: Mangystau Region (Caspian steppe/desert, near Kuryk port)
sites.capacityGW: ~40 GW (≈20 GW wind + ≈30 GW solar nameplate feeding 20 GW electrolysis)
sites.annualTWh: ~120 TWh/yr planned
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Project-stage; strong Caspian wind + S-Europe-class solar imply low LCOE (~$25-45/MWh)
sites.whyStranded: 40 GW planned in a sparsely populated Caspian desert region whose local demand is tiny; Kazakhstan's total renewables today are only ~2.9 GW. Output is intended for export green hydrogen/ammonia via Kuryk port. Weak local grid and demand make multi-GW renewable build effectively stranded without the H2 export or new compute load.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: strong complementary wind+solar (near-offshore-class Caspian wind), cool-to-cold continental climate cuts cooling energy, Caspian seawater available for cooling near coast, very cheap land. Cons: water-scarce desert interior, limited fiber/connectivity, landlocked routing, governance/financing and water-rights concerns, harsh continental temperature extremes.
sites.source: Eurasianet (Kazakhstan green-H2 west); Ammonia Energy Association (Hyrasia One); Hyrasia One project page

sites.name: US Southwest Desert Solar Belt (Mojave / Sonoran / Chihuahuan)
sites.region: SE California (Mojave), Arizona (Sonoran), W Texas / New Mexico (Chihuahuan)
sites.capacityGW: Multi-GW projects in pipeline (e.g. Bellefield ~1.5 GW, Discovery ~1.4 GW); regional technical potential >hundreds of GW
sites.annualTWh: Tens to hundreds of TWh/yr of additional potential
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ERCOT/SW solar PPAs ~$35-45/MWh (cheapest US region); national solar PPA index ~$58-62/MWh in 2025 (rising on tariffs)
sites.whyStranded: Not stranded in the export sense, but California/SW midday solar routinely exceeds local demand, producing negative prices and ~curtailment in CAISO; West Texas (ERCOT) similarly sees congestion and curtailment. Cheap surplus daytime power and transmission bottlenecks make these zones prime for co-located compute that soaks up otherwise-curtailed energy. AWS already signed a 15-yr PPA with the 1.5 GW Bellefield project.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheapest US solar, deep capital/hyperscaler presence, strong fiber backbones, stable jurisdiction, AI datacenter rush already underway in AZ/TX. Cons: extreme desert heat (Phoenix/Mojave 45C+) raises cooling load; severe water stress (Colorado River) constrains evaporative cooling — pushing operators (Microsoft etc.) to zero-water / liquid + air designs; solar is daytime-only, requiring storage or grid firming for 24x7 load.
sites.source: LevelTen North America PPA Price Index; Wikipedia Solar power plants in the Mojave Desert; Grist (Arizona water & datacenters)

caveats: Coordinates are representative centroids of each resource region/project, not exact facility footprints (especially for multi-site or pre-development zones like the Gobi, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, US SW, and Northern Cape). Capacity and TWh figures mix three different categories that should not be compared head-to-head: (1) operating plants with firm numbers (Noor Ouarzazate, Sudair, Al Dhafra, Benban); (2) under-construction/planned projects with announced targets that frequently slip or get rescoped (NEOM, Sun Cable/AAPowerLink, AREH Pilbara, Hyphen Namibia, Boegoebaai, Hyrasia One — note BP exited AREH and the UK declined the Xlinks CfD); and (3) theoretical resource potentials for whole regions (Mongolia Gobi ~2,600 TWh/yr; China Gobi ~455 GW; US SW). LCOE/PPA figures are time-stamped and not apples-to-apples: record bids ($10-13/MWh in Saudi/UAE, ~$27-33/MWh China) are stripped, daytime-only, often subsidized solar tariffs, while delivered/export prices (Xlinks ~GBP48/MWh, Sun Cable to Singapore) include thousands of km of HVDC and are far higher; US PPA index prices ($58-62/MWh, 2025) rose on tariffs. Annual TWh estimates I computed from nameplate x assumed capacity factors are order-of-magnitude only. 'Stranded' is used loosely: some sites (Al Dhafra, US SW) have strong grids but exhibit curtailment/negative-price surplus rather than true isolation, whereas others (Mongolia, Namibia, NT outback) are genuinely demand- and transmission-isolated. The single most important datacenter constraint across nearly all hot-desert sites is water for cooling: freshwater is scarce or absent, pushing operators toward seawater (NEOM, Hyphen, Boegoebaai, coastal AREH), dry/liquid cooling, or zero-water designs. Cooler high-latitude/coastal deserts (Mongolia Gobi, Namibia/Atlantic coast, Kazakhstan Caspian) are thermally more favorable than equatorial Gulf/Sahara/Pilbara sites but are weaker on connectivity. Saudi national renewable share is reported by different sources as ~2% (Ember, generation basis) vs. larger tendered/installed pipeline figures — treat grid-share numbers cautiously. Several sources are project developers, encyclopedias, or trade press rather than peer-reviewed/independent data; capacity and price claims should be re-verified against primary regulator/IEA/IRENA/BNEF data before any siting decision.

category: Remote mega-hydropower sites worldwide with stranded or hard-to-evacuate power, evaluated as candidates for co-located AI compute

sites.name: Medog (Motuo) Hydropower Station, Yarlung Tsangpo Great Bend
sites.region: Medog County, Nyingchi Prefecture, Tibet Autonomous Region (lower Yarlung Tsangpo / Great Bend around Namcha Barwa)
sites.capacityGW: ~60 GW (planned, five cascade dams; single-phase build started 19 Jul 2025)
sites.annualTWh: ~300 TWh/yr planned (~3x Three Gorges)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: no project figure published; benchmark new large hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024 global weighted avg). Likely higher here given extreme terrain/tunneling, but very low marginal cost once built
sites.whyStranded: Extreme remoteness on the contested India border at >2,000-3,000 m terrain; 300 TWh dwarfs local Tibetan demand (Tibet population/industry tiny). Power must be evacuated thousands of km east to load centers via long UHV DC lines that are not yet built; seasonal flow and the sheer scale create large surplus relative to any plausible local offtake until transmission and demand catch up to ~2033 commissioning.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool high-altitude climate reduces cooling load; abundant cheap firm power; latency to East Asian users acceptable. Cons: severe seismicity (Himalayan syntaxis, near 1950 Assam-Tibet quake zone), extreme remoteness and weak existing fiber/road access, very high altitude (reduced air density hurts air cooling and disk/component reliability), militarily sensitive border location, landslide/glacial-lake-outburst hazards.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Medog Hydropower Station'; The Diplomat (2026) 'What's Driving China's Mega Medog Hydropower Project?'; NetZeroCompare; Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon coords (Wikipedia)

sites.name: Grand Inga (Inga III + Grand Inga complex), Inga Falls
sites.region: Kongo Central Province, Congo River ~150 km upstream of the Atlantic, Inga Falls
sites.capacityGW: Inga III ~4.8 GW (first phase); full Grand Inga ~40 GW (up to 70 GW in some scenarios)
sites.annualTWh: Grand Inga theoretical potential ~270-370 TWh/yr at 40-70 GW; Inga III ~30 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: site has world-class low-cost potential (~$30-60/MWh range cited historically) but stalled financing and risk premiums raise effective cost; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: DRC domestic grid is tiny and unreliable (national access <25%); the resource vastly exceeds local demand. Output is premised on exporting 2.5 GW to South Africa, ~3 GW to Nigeria, and ~1.3 GW to Katanga mines via thousands of km of HVDC that does not yet exist. The Pan-African grid/HVLD lines are unbuilt, so power is structurally stranded; the project has been repeatedly stalled for decades.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: enormous, very low-cost, year-round firm hydro at a single site; tropical river provides cooling water. Cons: hot/humid equatorial climate raises cooling energy; minimal fiber/connectivity and grid infrastructure; high political/governance risk and currency risk in DRC; project execution risk extreme; would require captive build-out of all enabling infrastructure.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Grand Inga Dam' and 'Inga dams'; World Bank Inga III factsheet (2024) and press release (Jun 2025)

sites.name: Belo Monte Hydroelectric Plant, Xingu River
sites.region: Pará State, northern Brazil (Amazon basin), Xingu River near Altamira
sites.capacityGW: 11.2 GW installed (run-of-river)
sites.annualTWh: ~39 TWh/yr typical; assured 'firm' output far below nameplate — best case ~4.5 GW average (~39 TWh), and only ~4.46 GW average under favorable scenarios per studies
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~$40-60/MWh range typical for Brazilian large hydro; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Deep in the Amazon far from southeast load centers; ~90% of output is wheeled ~2,000+ km south via two dedicated 800 kV HVDC lines (built by State Grid/China). Huge capacity factor gap (run-of-river, small reservoir, dry-season collapse) leaves nameplate stranded most of the year, while distance creates evacuation cost and transmission losses. Cons: hot/humid tropical climate (high cooling load); strong run-of-river seasonality means firm power is far below nameplate; remote Amazon location with limited tier-1 fiber; environmental/social opposition and indigenous-land sensitivities.

sites.name: Madeira River Complex (Santo Antônio + Jirau)
sites.region: Rondônia State, Madeira River near Porto Velho (western Amazon, near Bolivia border)
sites.capacityGW: ~6.5 GW combined (Santo Antônio ~3.15 GW + Jirau ~3.3 GW), both run-of-river
sites.annualTWh: designed ~3 GW average each; actual generation a fraction of design due to climate/low-storage run-of-river operation; combined ~30-40 TWh/yr order of magnitude with high variability
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: ~$40-60/MWh typical Brazilian large hydro; benchmark ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)

Run-of-river with negligible storage means power can collapse in dry years and the plants produce well below design; local demand in Rondônia is small. sites.name: Siberian Angara–Yenisei cascade (Bratsk, Krasnoyarsk, Boguchany, + Ust-Ilimsk)
sites.region: Irkutsk Oblast & Krasnoyarsk Krai, Angara and Yenisei Rivers, south-central Siberia
sites.capacityGW: Bratsk 4.5 GW + Krasnoyarsk 6.0 GW + Boguchany 3.0 GW = ~13.5 GW (plus Ust-Ilimsk ~3.8 GW)
sites.annualTWh: Bratsk ~22.6 TWh + Krasnoyarsk ~18.4 TWh + Boguchany ~17.6 TWh = ~58.6 TWh/yr (cascade group)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: very low marginal cost (legacy Soviet-era amortized dams); effective ~$10-30/MWh internal transfer to smelters; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Power sits in the Siberian Unified grid which is weakly connected to European-Russia load centers; surplus has historically been absorbed by captive RUSAL aluminum smelters (Krasnoyarsk, Bratsk, Boguchany) precisely because it cannot be economically evacuated west. A crypto-mining crackdown and smelter cycles have freed gigawatts; the region is far from major domestic demand, leaving cheap firm power locally underused.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: very cheap firm hydro, sub-zero ambient temperatures enable free-cooling much of the year, gigawatts of freed capacity, low latency to China (Beijing/Harbin) vs SE Asia. Cons: severe Western sanctions and political/sectoral risk (chip access, financing); limited international fiber; cold-region construction/operations challenges; opaque grid pricing.
sites.source: NS Energy 'Russia's top five hydroelectric power plants'; Power-Technology Boguchany; Wikipedia 'Bratsk HPS'; bne IntelliNews (Siberia AI hub); DCD/Bloomberg on Irkutsk hydro data centers

sites.name: Churchill Falls Generating Station (+ Labrador/Gull Island potential)
sites.region: Labrador, Newfoundland and Labrador (Churchill River); power flows to Quebec border
sites.capacityGW: 5.43 GW (Churchill Falls); planned Gull Island + Churchill expansion under 2024 MOU could add several GW more
sites.annualTWh: ~34 TWh/yr
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: fully amortized; sold to Hydro-Québec under the 1969 contract at ~0.2 Canadian cents/kWh (~$1.5-2/MWh) until 2041 — among the cheapest power on earth; true marginal cost ~$5-15/MWh
sites.whyStranded: Classic stranded-asset case: ~90% of output is locked into the 1969 Quebec contract at ~0.2 cents/kWh because Labrador has almost no local load and the only transmission route runs ~200 km south into Quebec's grid (Newfoundland/Labrador long lacked alternative evacuation). Remote subarctic location, tiny local demand, and contractual/transmission lock-in mean the value is captured downstream, not locally.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: extremely cheap firm hydro, cold subarctic climate (free cooling nearly year-round), politically stable Canada, water abundant. Cons: very remote (low population, limited fiber/connectivity), harsh winters and short construction season, existing output contractually committed to 2041, limited local grid headroom until expansion built.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Churchill Falls Generating Station'; Globe and Mail (Dec 2024 deal); CBC; Hydro-Québec

sites.name: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Blue Nile
sites.region: Benishangul-Gumuz Region, Guba, Blue Nile near Sudan border
sites.capacityGW: 5.15 GW (13 Francis turbines; fully inaugurated 9 Sep 2025)
sites.annualTWh: ~15.8 TWh/yr design average
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: low-cost (state-financed); typical African large hydro ~$40-70/MWh; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Designed to roughly double national generation, far exceeding Ethiopia's near-term domestic demand and grid absorption. Surplus is meant for export to Sudan, Kenya, Djibouti, Tanzania, but regional interconnectors and offtake are still maturing; weak domestic transmission and demand leave a large exportable surplus that is hard to fully use. Located in a remote, geopolitically sensitive border region (Nile water disputes with Egypt/Sudan).
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: large new block of cheap renewable power; moderate-elevation climate; Ethiopia actively courting energy-intensive loads. Cons: limited international fiber/connectivity and weak grid reliability; geopolitical tension over Nile waters; remote border siting; currency/political risk; cooling water tied to contested river flows.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam'; Webuild Group; Water Power Magazine; African Sustainability Matters (inauguration Sep 2025)

sites.name: Itaipu Binacional, Paraná River
sites.region: Paraná River on the Brazil–Paraguay border, near Foz do Iguaçu / Ciudad del Este
sites.capacityGW: 14.0 GW (20 x 700 MW units)
sites.annualTWh: ~83.8 TWh (2023); historic peak 103.1 TWh (2016)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: debt largely paid off in 2023, so cost has dropped sharply — effectively ~$15-40/MWh going forward; among the cheapest large blocks in South America
sites.whyStranded: Paraguay owns half the output but uses only ~10% of total — its surplus has historically been sold to Brazil because Paraguay's small economy cannot absorb it and it cannot easily export elsewhere. The 2023 treaty-financial expiry reopened how the large Paraguayan surplus is priced/allocated, creating a structurally underused, very low-cost block on the Paraguayan side seeking new offtake.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: huge, now near-zero-marginal-cost firm hydro; large idle Paraguayan share; reasonable connectivity near a tri-border urban area; Paraguay actively marketing surplus to crypto/data loads. Cons: humid subtropical climate (moderate cooling load); Paraguay political/regulatory uncertainty post-2023 treaty; allocation of surplus contested between the two countries.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Itaipu Dam'; IEEE Spectrum; Power-Technology; Itaipu Binacional

sites.name: Cahora Bassa Dam, Zambezi River
sites.region: Tete Province, Zambezi River, northwestern Mozambique
sites.capacityGW: 2.075 GW (5 x ~415 MW Francis turbines)
sites.annualTWh: ~14-16 TWh/yr design; ~10.9 TWh in 2021 (drought-reduced)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: amortized legacy plant, low cost ~$20-40/MWh; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Most output (~66% of deliveries) is exported to South Africa's Eskom over a dedicated >1,400 km HVDC line (the world's first ±533 kV scheme) because Mozambique's domestic grid cannot absorb it — northern Mozambique demand is tiny and the national grid is fragmented. The dam's value is captured downstream in South Africa, and the HVDC was even idle 1985-1997 during civil war, underscoring evacuation fragility.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cheap firm hydro, abundant Zambezi cooling water, existing high-capacity HVDC corridor. Cons: hot climate (high cooling load); drought-driven generation variability; weak domestic fiber/grid; remote Tete location; Mozambique political/security risk (northern insurgency elsewhere in country) and currency risk.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Cahora Bassa Dam'; Britannica; ESMAP case study; REN (Portugal)

sites.name: HidroAysén (Baker & Pascua Rivers), Patagonia
sites.region: Aysén Region, Chilean Patagonia (Baker and Pascua Rivers)
sites.capacityGW: 2.75 GW (5 dams, cancelled 2014; resource remains)
sites.annualTWh: ~18-20 TWh/yr would have been generated (project would have supplied 15-20% of Chile's needs)
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: would-be low-cost hydro ~$50-80/MWh, but a ~2,000 km transmission line to Santiago load center dominated cost and killed economics; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: The defining stranded-by-transmission case: the resource sits in deep Patagonia ~1,900-2,300 km from Chile's central load (Santiago), and the project was cancelled in 2014 largely because the long transmission corridor was prohibitively costly and contested. Local Aysén demand is negligible, so the hydro potential is effectively stranded by distance — exactly the profile where on-site compute could substitute for a transmission line.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool/cold Patagonian climate ideal for free cooling; abundant water; stable Chile; very strong renewable resource if developed. Cons: project legally cancelled and politically toxic (strong environmental opposition); extreme remoteness with almost no fiber backbone; no existing transmission; would require greenfield build of all infrastructure and new permitting; seismically active region.
sites.source: Enerdata; International Rivers (cancellation); National Geographic; EJAtlas

sites.name: Nepal Himalayan hydropower (national run-of-river fleet + potential)
sites.region: Himalayan and mid-hill river basins (e.g., Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali), central Nepal
sites.capacityGW: ~3-4 GW installed and rising; ~42 GW technically/economically viable; ~83 GW theoretical
sites.annualTWh: wet-season surplus already causes spillage; viable potential could yield well over 150-200 TWh/yr if fully built; current generation far smaller
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: Nepali run-of-river ~$40-70/MWh; spilled wet-season energy has near-zero opportunity cost when export-constrained; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Run-of-river fleet produces large monsoon-season surpluses that cannot be stored or fully consumed domestically. In 2025 the wet-season surplus (~1,400 MW) exceeded India's export approval (~1,141 MW), forcing spillage/curtailment at NEA plants. Transmission to India is the only export route and is approval- and capacity-constrained, so wet-season energy is literally spilled — classic curtailed/strandable energy.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool mid-hill/Himalayan climate aids cooling; genuinely curtailed wet-season energy available cheaply; growing fiber via India. Cons: highly seasonal (dry-season deficit means firm power is scarce without storage); severe Himalayan seismicity and GLOF/landslide risk; difficult mountainous terrain and limited grid/fiber redundancy; dependence on India for connectivity and export.
sites.source: Kathmandu Post (2023, 2025 spillage); IPPAN; International Water Power; NREL cross-border trade report

sites.name: Bhutan Himalayan hydropower (Tala, Chukha, Punatsangchhu, Mangdechhu)
sites.region: Inner-Himalayan river valleys (Wangchhu/Tala, Punatsangchhu, Mangdechhu basins)
sites.capacityGW: ~2.46 GW installed (end-2024), almost entirely hydro; target 15 GW hydro by 2040
sites.annualTWh: ~10.5 TWh/yr (2023); ~5.1 TWh exported to India in 2023
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: low-cost run-of-river ~$30-60/MWh; export priced to India bilaterally; wet-season surplus has low marginal value; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Bhutan's hydro is overwhelmingly run-of-river and seasonal: it generates large monsoon surpluses sold almost exclusively to India (the only interconnected market), then must import in winter. Surplus is structurally dependent on a single export buyer and inter-tie capacity; domestic demand only recently approached export volumes. Wet-season energy is effectively strandable beyond what India will take.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: cool Himalayan climate, very high renewable share, stable governance, Bhutan explicitly courting compute/crypto and green-hydrogen loads to monetize surplus. Cons: strong seasonality (winter deficits, run-of-river); Himalayan seismicity/GLOF risk; landlocked with limited fiber routes (via India); small grid and single-buyer export dependence.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Energy in Bhutan'; ADB 'Bhutan's Hydropower Sector: 12 Things to Know'; World Bank Dorjilung financing

sites.name: Rogun Hydropower Plant, Vakhsh River
sites.region: Vakhsh River, Pamir foothills, central Tajikistan (south of Dushanbe)
sites.capacityGW: ~3.6-3.78 GW (6 units; will be world's tallest dam at 335 m; partial operation underway, full completion later this decade)
sites.annualTWh: ~17 TWh/yr at full build
sites.lcoeUSDperMWh: new-build large hydro ~$40-70/MWh; very low marginal cost once complete; benchmark hydro ~$57/MWh (IRENA 2024)
sites.whyStranded: Tajikistan already has winter shortages but big summer surpluses; Rogun's output far exceeds domestic demand in summer. The export plan hinges on the CASA-1000 line (~1,300 MW) to Afghanistan and Pakistan, which is delayed (now targeted ~Dec 2026) and complicated by Afghan instability. Until CASA-1000 and storage operate, large summer hydro surpluses are stranded in a small, weakly interconnected Central Asian grid far from any large stable buyer.
sites.datacenterSuitability: Pros: very cheap future firm hydro, mountainous cool climate aids cooling, surplus summer energy seeking offtake. Cons: extreme seismicity (record-height dam in active zone) and dam-safety scrutiny; severe winter domestic deficits (firm power not guaranteed); minimal international fiber; landlocked with regional security risk (Afghanistan); reliance on delayed CASA-1000 corridor.
sites.source: Wikipedia 'Rogun Dam'; NS Energy & Power-Technology 'Rogun'; World Bank CASA-1000 risk assessment; APP (CASA-1000 timeline)

caveats: Coordinates are approximate centroids of the project/resource region (decimal degrees) derived from public descriptions, not surveyed dam-axis points; verify before any siting use. Capacity and generation figures mix nameplate (installed) with average annual output — for run-of-river Amazon and Himalayan plants the gap is large, and firm/dispatchable power is far below nameplate (Belo Monte averages ~4.5 GW vs 11.2 GW nameplate; Nepal/Bhutan/Rogun swing seasonally). LCOE is the weakest data point: almost none of these projects publish a project-specific levelized cost, so I anchored to IRENA's 2024 global weighted-average new-hydro LCOE of ~$57/MWh (USD 0.057/kWh) and noted that legacy amortized dams (Churchill Falls, Itaipu post-2023, Siberian cascade, Cahora Bassa) have far lower effective/marginal costs while greenfield extreme-terrain projects (Medog, Rogun, Inga) likely run higher; treat all $/MWh values as order-of-magnitude. 'Stranded' is used in the practical sense of power that is hard to use locally or costly to evacuate — including contractual lock-in (Churchill Falls), single-buyer export dependence (Bhutan, Cahora Bassa, GERD), curtailment/spillage (Nepal), transmission-gap (Inga, HidroAysén, Rogun/CASA-1000), and capacity-factor shortfall (Amazon). HidroAysén is legally cancelled (2014) and is listed as 'potential' for the resource only. Status and figures are current to ~early 2026; several projects (Medog, GERD turbines, Rogun, Inga III, Churchill Falls expansion) are fast-moving — reconfirm before relying on specifics. Datacenter suitability is a qualitative screen (climate/cooling, water, altitude, seismicity, fiber, political/sanctions risk), not an engineering site assessment; sanctions on Russia and DRC/Afghanistan-area governance/security risk are first-order disqualifiers for many operators despite favorable power. Primary sources cited are Wikipedia, IRENA, World Bank, ADB, and trade/news outlets (NS Energy, Power-Technology, The Diplomat, Kathmandu Post, Globe and Mail, Enerdata); for rigorous use, cross-check against owner/operator filings and national system-operator data.
